nameStory: The 'pin-cushion' part of this lichen's name comes from its bumpy, textured surface covered in tiny raised fruiting bodies that look like pins stuck into a cushion. The 'sunburst' refers to the bright yellow-orange color that radiates outward like rays of sunshine, which is characteristic of many lichens in this family.
description: Pin-cushion Sunburst Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that grows flat against tree bark, forming bright yellow-orange patches. A lichen is actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae - that work as a team to survive on tree trunks and branches. This particular species creates colorful, crusty patches that can brighten up the bark of deciduous trees. The surface is dotted with small, raised bumps that give it that distinctive pin-cushion texture.

idTips.label: Bright yellow-orange color
idTips.description: Look for vibrant golden-yellow to orange patches that stand out boldly against dark bark - much brighter than most other lichens

idTips.label: Pin-cushion texture
idTips.description: Feel the surface gently - it's bumpy with many small, raised dots (fruiting bodies) that create a textured, almost granular feeling

idTips.label: Leafy growth pattern
idTips.description: Grows as overlapping, leaf-like lobes that lie flat against the bark rather than standing upright or forming crusts

idTips.label: Bark-dwelling habit
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on tree bark, never on rocks or soil - press gently and feel how it's firmly attached to the bark surface

idTips.label: Patch formation
idTips.description: Forms distinct circular or irregular patches rather than covering large areas uniformly, often with clear edges where it meets bare bark

habitat: Pin-cushion Sunburst Lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas. It particularly favors trees with relatively smooth bark and seems to thrive in areas with good air circulation but some protection from the harshest weather. You'll often spot it on maples, oaks, and other hardwood trees at various elevations from sea level to mid-mountain forests.

seasonality.spring: The bright yellow-orange color becomes more vibrant as temperatures warm and moisture increases, making this an excellent time for spotting this colorful lichen against awakening tree bark.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen may appear slightly duller but the pin-cushion texture of fruiting bodies is often most pronounced and easy to feel.
seasonality.fall: The golden colors really pop against the changing autumn foliage, and this is often when the lichen is most photogenic and noticeable to casual observers.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable on bare tree trunks, though colors may be somewhat muted - the textured surface remains the most reliable identifying feature in cold weather.

funFact: This lichen has been through more name changes than a witness protection program participant - it has acquired 'quite an extensive synonymy' according to scientists, meaning it's been renamed and reclassified so many times that researchers have a long list of former names to keep track of!
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with other bright yellow-orange lichens in the sunburst family, but the pin-cushion texture sets it apart - if you can feel those distinctive raised bumps, you've likely found the right species. Memory trick: 'Pin-cushion texture, pin-cushion name!'
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved to the genus Polycauliona in 2013 as part of a major reorganization of lichen classification based on DNA studies, so you might find it listed under older names in field guides published before that date.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Ringed Firedot Lichen and Shrubby Sunburst Lichen, Pin-cushion Sunburst Lichen has that distinctive bumpy, textured surface with numerous small raised fruiting bodies. While all three species share the bright yellow-orange coloration typical of this group, the pin-cushion texture is unique to this species and makes it relatively easy to distinguish once you know what to feel for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its inland cousins like Pin-cushion Sunburst Lichen and Shrubby Sunburst Lichen, Ringed Firedot sticks strictly to coastal rocks and has a flatter, more tightly attached growth form.
Shrubby Sunburst Lichen differs from its close relative Pin-cushion Sunburst Lichen by having a more irregular, branching growth pattern rather than neat cushion-like bumps.
